title: Stages of life
hook: Hindu tradition names four stages of life, from student to renunciant

segments.voice: Yesterday, work and home, and the question from Ecclesiastes: who is all this labor for? Your line was they're waiting. Did you pick your day to leave on time? Today, a map that asks what work is for at each point in a life. Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

A student cramming for exams wants to know why nobody will let her just get on with her life. A parent can't remember the last time the house was quiet. A man, newly retired, stands in the kitchen at ten in the morning and has no idea what he's for. Each of them is asking the same question at a different hour: what is this part of my life supposed to be about? Hindu tradition has an old answer. It doesn't give one rule for a whole life. It gives four. Today's word: ashrama.
screen: `A STUDENT, A PARENT, A RETIREE.` → `WHAT IS THIS PART FOR?` → `FOUR STAGES.`

segments.voice: First, the four. In Hindu tradition, the ashramas are stages of life. In the student stage, brahmacharya, a young person learns from a teacher. In the householder stage, grihastha, a person marries, works, raises a family and keeps a home. In the forest stage, vanaprastha, the forest dweller steps back from the busy middle of life. And in sannyasa, the renunciant lets go of home and possessions altogether. Second, the hinge. The Laws of Manu, an old Hindu law book, gives a picture of when to move on. In paraphrase: when a householder sees his skin wrinkled, his hair white, and the sons of his sons, he may go to the forest. Not a birthday. Grandchildren and gray hair. The sign isn't a number. It's that the next generation has arrived. Third, the householder's honor. It would be easy to hear the stages as a ladder, with the renunciant at the top and the busy parent at the bottom. Manu says something different about the middle. It compares the householder to the air: as all creatures live by the air, the other stages live by the householder's support. The student is fed, the wanderer is given alms, because someone is working and keeping a home. In this picture, work is not a detour from the spiritual life. For a season, it is the spiritual life. Fourth, a map, not a cage. The old texts were written for men of particular classes, and Hindus read and live the stages in different ways today. Some see them as a strict pattern, some as a loose map. What the map offers anyone is a question: not what is life for, but what is this stage for?
screen: `STUDENT, HOUSEHOLDER, FOREST, RENUNCIANT.` · `GRAY HAIR AND GRANDCHILDREN.` · `ALL LIVE BY THE HOUSEHOLDER.` · `A MAP, NOT A CAGE.` · then, large: `ASHRAMA.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Hear the four names again: student, householder, forest dweller, renunciant. Without judging, ask which one describes this season of your life. Maybe more than one. Maybe you're a householder still taking notes like a student, or a worker already stepping back. Name your stage, quietly, to yourself. Then ask one more question: what does this stage ask of me? Not forever. Just now. Let one plain answer come, and stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Ashrama. A stage of life in Hindu tradition: student, householder, forest dweller, renunciant, each with its own work. Today's word.
Your line: my stage. Today, when work asks something of you, check it against your answer: is this what my stage is for? Day nine hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Hindus who follow the ashrama pattern treat each stage as having its own duties: study for the student, work and family for the householder, a gradual stepping back for the forest dweller, and renunciation for those who take sannyasa.

notes: Audit: the teach and match game named the people ('the student, brahmacharya') with the names of the stages; brahmacharya, grihastha, vanaprastha and sannyasa are the stages (the persons are brahmachari, grihastha, vanaprasthi, sannyasi), so both now say 'the student stage' etc.

Editor: removed the invented ages (twenty, forty, sixty) from the hook per the claims rule; added Manu 6.87 (which names the four orders) as the source for 'it gives four'; framed 'work is the spiritual life' as Manu's picture, not the narrator's claim.

Manu 6.2 paraphrased (Bühler 1886 has 'When a householder sees his (skin) wrinkled, and (his hair) white, and the sons of his sons, then he may resort to the forest'); Bühler is public domain but not on the validator's list, so paraphrased. Confirm.
Manu 3.77 (householder compared to air) paraphrased; 3.78's ranking of the householder order is deliberately not stated as a superlative.
'The old texts were written for men of particular classes' (the twice-born): a Hindu Keeper should check this framing is fair and sufficient.
Transliterations and Devanagari आश्रम; pronunciation AH-shruh-muh. Confirm.
